sentences.text: The genus name Ornithoprion translates from Greek as 'bird saw', referring to the bird-like skull and saw-like lower jaw teeth. This animal possessed a lower jaw tooth arrangement called a tooth whorl, which looked like a saw and featured up to seven broad, rounded tooth crowns.
Many dermal denticles on Ornithoprion fused into compound scales called polyodontode scales, featuring a single base with up to seven crowns.
Most known specimens are preserved on their side and are flattened, including the holotype.
Due to the shape of the Meckel's cartilages, the mouth of Ornithoprion was likely incapable of closing, although the mandibular rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages at a flexible joint.
Bite marks and damage on some fossils indicate that Ornithoprion was preyed upon by other carnivores.
The genus Ornithoprion was described by Rainer Zangerl in 1966.
Specimen FMNH PF-2710 from the Mecca Quarry was designated as the holotype of the species.
The study of the holotype and paratypes of Ornithoprion was primarily performed using radiographic imaging.
Zangerl suggested that the armor and jaw articulation of Ornithoprion's skull were shock-absorbing adaptations.
The mandibular rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages at a flexible joint.
Most other fish skeletons from the Logan Quarry show similar feeding traces or are preserved in fossilized regurgitates or coprolites.

Ornithoprion was originally classified in the family Edestidae, which was traditionally placed in the order Bradyodonti or the subclass Holocephali. Zangerl originally classified Ornithoprion and other edestids as elasmobranchs.
In 1981, Zangerl reclassified Ornithoprion into the family Caseodontidae, superfamily Caseodontoidea, and order Eugeneodontiformes. Ornithoprion is classified within the family Caseodontidae.
Ornithoprion is a distant relative of living sharks, despite sometimes being referred to as a shark.
The only known species, Ornithoprion hertwigi, lived during the Moscovian stage of the Pennsylvanian subperiod.
Ornithoprion fossils were found in deposits from the North American Midcontinent Sea, a large inland sea.
While Zangerl speculated that processes on the back of the cranium were a fused hyoid arch, this interpretation has been questioned by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen.

There is a debate regarding the attachment of Ornithoprion's upper teeth, with some researchers suggesting they attached to the underside of the cranium while others believe they attached to a fused portion of the palatoquadrates.

Roger S. Miles tentatively placed Ornithoprion in Holocephali but suggested its similarities to edestids resulted from convergent evolution due to differences in gill anatomy, tooth histology, and palatoquadrates.
While Zangerl's family and order classifications are still used, his view that eugeneodonts are elasmobranchs has been refuted; they are now considered a monophyletic group within Holocephali.
Some authors debate whether the shales containing Ornithoprion were formed in shallow water or deep-water environments.
